name: Capesize

size.n: Wikipedia (Bulk carrier, size categories, read in November 2026) puts Capesize at 80,000 dwt and over, and the very large ore and bulk carriers of over 200,000 dwt in a subset of their own. The Atlas starts the class at 85,000 dwt, where its Kamsarmax band ends, and ends it at 200,000 dwt, where its VLOC band starts; Newcastlemax is a port-defined class that sits inside this band and the next.

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's reference ship for its Capesize time-charter routes, with the figures of its dry services page: capacity in cubic metres of grain, fuel in tonnes a day at the speed shown.

constraints: Loads only at deep-water terminals
Cannot use Panama laden; routes via Cape of Good Hope/Cape Horn

canals.suez: Transits laden within SCA limits (max draft 20.1 m at beam up to 50 m)
canals.panama: Too wide for Panamax locks and laden draft exceeds the 15.24 m Neopanamax limit; does not transit laden

notes: Baltic standard vessel moved from 180,000 to 182,000 dwt (C5TC(182), effective 2 Jan 2026).

name: Newcastlemax

size.n: Wikipedia (Bulk carrier, read in November 2026) defines Newcastlemax by the port of Newcastle, Australia: at most 50 m beam and 300 m length overall, the largest vessel able to enter the port at about 185,000 dwt. That figure is the typical size. The band, 185,000 to 210,000 dwt, is an Atlas convention for ships built to the port's beam and length limits (no page read gives a band). The class sits inside the Capesize and VLOC bands: it is defined by a port, not by a size step.

constraints: Max LOA ~300 m, beam ~50 m (design limits at Newcastle)
Deep-water terminals only

canals.suez: Transits at the SCA beam limit (50 m beam allows 20.1 m draft); verify per vessel
canals.panama: Too wide for Panamax locks and laden draft exceeds the 15.24 m Neopanamax limit; does not transit laden

bench.n: Benchmarks: the Baltic Capesize routes, defined for a 182,000 dwt ship

notes: No Baltic benchmark uses this class: the Baltic Capesize routes, C5 (West Australia to Qingdao) among them, are defined for the Baltic Capesize vessel of 182,000 dwt. The Pilbara routes are listed because the atlas's lane rules give Newcastlemax as the second class of large Australian ore lanes; C5 and the Pilbara route stay Capesize routes. The typical size is the page's figure for the largest vessel the port takes (see Size band).

name: VLOC (Valemax/Guaibamax)

size.n: Wikipedia (Bulk carrier, read in November 2026): very large ore and bulk carriers are a subset of the Capesize category reserved for ships over 200,000 dwt. The upper end is the Valemax's 400,000 dwt (Wikipedia, Valemax: 380,000 to 400,000 dwt), which meets the Chinamax standard.

std.n: Not a Baltic standard vessel: the Valemax as Wikipedia (Valemax, read in November 2026) gives it, 380,000 to 400,000 dwt, 360 to 362 m long, about 65 m wide, 22 to 23 m loaded draught (about 12 m in ballast); the figures above are the upper deadweight and the lower length and draught.

constraints: Only a few ports can take them (e.g. Ponta da Madeira, Tubarao, Qingdao, Dalian, Rizhao, Rotterdam via Maasvlakte)
Valemax had a Chinese port ban until 2016, then restricted to approved berths

canals.suez: Cannot transit Suez laden (beam/draft beyond the SCA wetted-area limit)
canals.panama: Too wide for Panamax locks and laden draft exceeds the 15.24 m Neopanamax limit; does not transit laden

notes: Chinamax/Valemax ships are of about 400,000 dwt (Wikipedia, Valemax and Chinamax).

name: Panamax

size.n: Wikipedia (Panamax, read in November 2026): a Panamax cargo ship would typically have 65,000 to 80,000 dwt. (Wikipedia, Bulk carrier, starts the category at 60,000 dwt; the Atlas uses the Panamax article's band so that it does not overlap Ultramax.) The typical size, 74,000 dwt, is an Atlas convention: the size in the name of the Baltic's Panamax 74 time-charter average (P4TC), which the Baltic's Guide to Market Benchmarks (December 2025) derives from its 82,500 dwt routes without describing a 74,000 dwt vessel; the Baltic's Panamax vessel of the P*_82 routes is an 82,500 dwt ship, filed under Kamsarmax.

constraints: Draft limits at US Gulf river terminals, Up-River Parana and Columbia River restrict cargo size (cargo then topped off elsewhere)

canals.panama: Fits Panamax locks (design size: LOA 289.56 m, beam 32.31 m, TFW draft 12.04 m)

bench.n: Benchmarks: the Baltic Panamax routes, defined for an 82,500 dwt ship of Kamsarmax size

notes: The Baltic Panamax vessel of the benchmark routes (P1A_82, P2A_82, P3A_82, P6_82) is an 82,500 dwt ship of 229 m, which the atlas files under Kamsarmax by size; the routes are listed here too. The Atlas puts the class first on the lanes of Canadian potash above 2 Mt a year (an assumption: no page was read for the class of these lanes).

name: Kamsarmax

size.n: Wikipedia (Bulk carrier, read in November 2026) defines Kamsarmax by its 229 m length overall, the limit of the port of Kamsar, Guinea, not by deadweight. The band, 80,000 to 85,000 dwt, is an Atlas convention, from the upper end of Panamax (80,000 dwt, Wikipedia, Panamax) to the start of the Atlas's Capesize band.

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's reference ship for its Panamax time-charter routes (P*_82), with the figures of its dry services page: capacity in cubic metres of grain, fuel in tonnes a day at the speed shown.

constraints: 229 m LOA limit set by Kamsar port, Guinea

canals.panama: Beam fits Panamax locks (32.31 m) but laden draft typically exceeds the 12.04 m TFW limit; usually uses Neopanamax locks or goes via Suez/Cape

notes: The Baltic's Panamax vessel (P1A_82, P2A_82, P3A_82, P6_82) is an 82,500 dwt ship of 229 m: a Kamsarmax by size. The Atlas also puts the class first on the lanes of grains, oilseeds, meals, pulses and sugar that leave the United States, Brazil, Argentina, Canada or Australia above 1 Mt a year, which is why soybean meal, sugar, rapeseed and pulses are among the cargoes with the grains (an Atlas assumption: no page was read for the class of these lanes).

name: Supramax

size.n: Wikipedia (Handymax, version of 2025 read in November 2026): Supramax ships are of 50,000 to 60,000 dwt and Handymax ships of 40,000 to 50,000 dwt. The Atlas has no Handymax class (no lane rule of its own would use one): this class covers both, from 40,000 dwt, so that no size is left uncovered above Handysize.

constraints: Geared; used at ports lacking shore cranes

canals.panama: Transits Panamax locks (beam ~32 m, draft up to 12.04 m TFW)

bench.n: Benchmarks: the Baltic Supramax routes, defined for a 63,500 dwt ship of Ultramax size

notes: The typical size, 58,000 dwt, is an Atlas convention: the size in the name of the Baltic's Supramax 58 time-charter average (S10TC), which the Baltic's Guide to Market Benchmarks (December 2025) derives from its 63,500 dwt routes without describing a 58,000 dwt vessel. The Baltic's Standard Supramax is a 63,500 dwt ship, the size the atlas files under Ultramax. The Atlas also puts the class first on the lanes of ferrous scrap, chromite, pig iron, direct-reduced iron and coke (A-010; coke is a group of the Metallurgical coal page, which is why that page is in the list of cargoes), with the Handysize second, as for steel: parcels of a few tens of thousands of tonnes in geared handy bulk carriers. It is also first on the smaller flows of iron ore, bauxite, alumina, soybean meal and sugar and on the spodumene lanes (the rules of the vessel classes of the lanes). This is an Atlas assumption: no page was read for the class of these lanes.

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's reference ship for its Supramax time-charter routes (S*_63), with the figures of its dry services page: capacity in cubic metres of grain, fuel in tonnes a day at the speed shown.

constraints: Geared: the Baltic standard Supramax has four 30 t cranes with grabs

canals.panama: Transits Panamax locks (beam ~ 32 m, draft 12.04 m)

notes: Baltic standard Supramax moved to 63,500 dwt (BSI 63, Circular 09/23). The Baltic calls this 63,500 dwt ship its Standard Supramax, so its S*_63 routes are listed under Supramax too.

name: MR

size.n: An Atlas convention: from 40,000 dwt, where the Handy tanker band ends, to 55,000 dwt. The AFRA scale (Wikipedia, Oil tanker) puts Medium Range at 25,000 to 44,999 dwt; the Baltic Exchange's standard MR (MR50, 50,000 dwt, Guide to Market Benchmarks, December 2025) falls above it, which is why the Atlas starts the class at 40,000 dwt. Other published scales cut the classes differently. The typical size is the Baltic's standard MR.

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's standard MR for its clean tanker time-charter equivalents, from its Guide to Market Benchmarks: fuel oil in tonnes a day at the speed shown. No length, beam or draught is given.

constraints: Clean products: the Baltic's MR routes carry cargoes of 35,000 to 40,000 t

canals.panama: Fits Panamax locks

notes: The Baltic's standard MR is a 50,000 dwt ship; TC2_37 cargo 37,000 t, TC10 and TC11 40,000 t (Baltic Exchange, Guide to Market Benchmarks, December 2025). The Atlas puts the class first on vegetable-oil lanes: the Baltic assesses vegetable-oil freight basis 40,000 t shipments on chemical tankers (Baltic Chemical and Agricultural Oil Assessments), a cargo the size of the MR benchmark cargoes.

name: Handy tanker

size.n: An Atlas convention: 10,000 to 40,000 dwt, where MR starts. The AFRA scale (Wikipedia, Oil tanker) cuts this range into General Purpose (10,000 to 24,999 dwt) and Medium Range (25,000 to 44,999 dwt). The typical size is the Baltic Exchange's standard Handy tanker (37,800 dwt), from its Guide to Market Benchmarks (December 2025); the Baltic's Handy routes carry 30,000 t cargoes.

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's standard Handy tanker (clean and dirty versions alike) for its time-charter equivalents, from its guide: fuel oil in tonnes a day at the speed shown. No length, beam or draught is given.

name: Chemical tanker

size.n: Wikipedia (Chemical tanker, version of 2024 read in November 2026): oceangoing chemical tankers range from 5,000 to 35,000 dwt. A chemical tanker is a type of ship (tanks built, coated and cleaned for the cargoes of the International Bulk Chemical Code), not a size step, so its band overlaps the Handy tanker band. The typical size is the middle of the band, an Atlas convention.

constraints: Coated or stainless-steel tanks cleaned between cargoes; besides chemicals it carries palm oil, vegetable oils, tallow, caustic soda and methanol (Wikipedia, Chemical tanker)

The Baltic Exchange's chemical tanker assessments price vegetable oils basis 40,000 t shipments (Baltic Chemical and Agricultural Oil Assessments), a parcel larger than the largest chemical tanker of this band (35,000 dwt, Wikipedia, Chemical tanker)

canals.suez: No restriction applied by the Atlas rules (no sourced limit read)
canals.panama: No restriction applied by the Atlas rules (no sourced limit read)

notes: The Atlas puts the class second on vegetable-oil lanes (palm oil, soybean oil, and the sunflower and rapeseed oils of M-023), after the MR: the Baltic's 40,000 t vegetable-oil basis is larger than the largest chemical tanker on the Wikipedia scale (35,000 dwt) and the size of an MR cargo, which is why the MR comes first. Speed: the class has none of its own, so the default speed the Atlas assumes for such a class applies (see the assumed laden service speed). It is also first on the lanes of UAN solution (the Urea & nitrogen page) and of phosphoric acid (the Phosphate page), the Handy tanker second: liquids that are not dry bulk. This is an Atlas assumption: no page was read for the class of these lanes.

name: LNG carrier

size.n: Wikipedia (LNG carrier, read in November 2026): LNG carriers have grown to the Q-Max of up to 266,000 cbm; the Q-Flex and Q-Max carry 210,000 to 266,000 cbm. The lower end, 140,000 cbm, is an Atlas convention for the conventional carriers (no page read gives it); small-scale carriers below 40,000 cbm (same page) are not an Atlas class. The typical size is the Baltic's LNG carrier of the BLNG routes (174,000 cbm).

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's standard LNG carrier of its BLNG routes, from its Guide to Market Benchmarks: cargo capacity in cubic metres, fuel oil in tonnes a day at the speed shown; length and beam are approximate.

constraints: Conventional carrier of 174,000 cbm (the Baltic's BLNG routes); Q-Flex and Q-Max of 210,000 to 266,000 cbm (Wikipedia, LNG carrier), owned by Nakilat and chartered to Qatar's LNG producers (Wikipedia, Q-Flex and Q-Max)
Terminal draft and berth restrictions at some US/European terminals

canals.suez: Q-Max: Wikipedia (Q-Max) says the first Q-Max, Mozah, transited the canal for the first time days before it delivered its first cargo, 266,000 cbm, at Bilbao in January 2009; the page implies a laden transit. The Atlas checks the Q-Max's 53.8 m beam at about 12 m draft (Wikipedia, Q-Max), about 645 m2, against the canal's wetted-area limit of 1,006 m2 (Wikipedia, Suezmax). Conventional carriers and Q-Flex: no restriction applied by the Atlas rules
canals.panama: Conventional carriers use the Neopanamax locks (the Baltic's BLNG3 route, US Gulf to Japan, is defined via the Panama Canal); the Q-Max's 53.8 m beam (Wikipedia, Q-Max) is wider than the 51.25 m of the Neopanamax locks (Wikipedia, Panamax). No beam of a Q-Flex was read

notes: The Atlas has no separate Q-Flex or Q-Max class: they are LNG carriers of the Qatari trades, and no lane rule would use them apart from the class as a whole.

name: VLGC

size.n: Wilhelmsen (LPG vessel management, read in November 2026): very large gas carriers are LPG ships of 70,000 cbm and above. The upper end, 100,000 cbm, is an Atlas convention. Large gas carriers (50,000 to 70,000 cbm, same page) are not an Atlas class: no lane rule uses them, so the bands leave that step out. The typical size is the Baltic Exchange's standard LPG carrier of the LPG routes (VLGC84, 84,000 cbm), from its Guide to Market Benchmarks (December 2025).

std.n: The Baltic Exchange's standard LPG carrier of its BLPG routes, from its Guide to Market Benchmarks: cargo capacity in cubic metres, fuel oil in tonnes a day at the speed shown.

constraints: Fully refrigerated LPG carrier; Neopanamax-size (beam > 32.31 m)

canals.panama: Neopanamax locks only; too wide for Panamax locks

notes: The Baltic LPG time-charter equivalents are based on a VLGC of 84,000 cbm (VLGC84); BLPG parcel 44,000 t (Baltic Exchange, Guide to Market Benchmarks, December 2025).

name: Mid-size gas carrier

size.n: Wilhelmsen (LPG vessel management, read in November 2026): mid-size, fully refrigerated LPG ships of 25,000 to 50,000 cbm, used on intra-regional routes and medium-haul cross-trades. The typical size is the middle of the band, an Atlas convention.

constraints: Fully refrigerated LPG carrier, smaller than a VLGC; serves regional LPG trades and short hauls

canals.suez: No restriction applied by the Atlas rules (no sourced limit read)
canals.panama: No restriction applied by the Atlas rules (no sourced limit read)

notes: Band as a ship manager states it for its mid-size, fully refrigerated LPG ships (25,000 to 50,000 cbm); other published scales cut the gas-carrier classes differently. The typical size is the middle of the band, an Atlas convention: no typical size was read. The Atlas puts the class first on LPG lanes shorter than 1,000 nm, and on lanes under 3,000 nm that load less than one VLGC parcel a week (44 kt x 52); the two distances are Atlas assumptions. Speed: the class has none of its own, so the default speed the Atlas assumes for such a class applies (see the assumed laden service speed). The Atlas also puts it first on ammonia lanes (the Urea & nitrogen page), the VLGC second: ammonia is a refrigerated liquid carried in gas carriers like LPG. This is an Atlas assumption: no page was read for the class of ammonia lanes.

name: Container ship

size.n: Wikipedia (Container ship, read in November 2026): size categories from small feeders of up to 1,000 TEU to ultra-large ships of 14,501 TEU and more, and a capacity of up to 24,000 TEU in the infobox. The typical size is the middle of the band, an Atlas convention that describes no single lane.

constraints: Carries cargo in standard containers, not in bulk; ships under 3,000 TEU are called feeders and mostly serve smaller container ports

canals.suez: No restriction applied by the Atlas rules (no sourced limit read for the class as a whole)
canals.panama: No restriction applied by the Atlas rules (no sourced limit read for the class as a whole)

notes: Size band from the Wikipedia article Container ship (read in November 2026; CC BY-SA 4.0): its size categories run from small feeders of up to 1,000 TEU to ultra-large ships of 14,501 TEU and more, and its infobox gives a capacity of up to 24,000 TEU, so the range starts at 0 and ends at 24,000. The page gives no typical size: the typical size is the middle of the band, an Atlas convention that describes no single lane. The Atlas uses the class first for general cargo that moves in boxes (refined copper, aluminium, coffee, cocoa, cotton, refined lead and zinc, tin, lithium, cobalt, the rare earths and the ferro-alloys), with the Handysize second; it is a stand-in for the whole container fleet, not a measured share. The page's canal figures (Panama locks, Suez) belong to particular size categories, so no restriction is applied to the class as a whole. Speed: see the assumed laden service speed.
